1  Introduction
In the dynamic and rapidly transforming field of logistics and 
warehousing, the integration of industrial fog and mobile 
edge computing technologies is significantly enhancing the 
efficiency and accuracy of real-time automated identifica­
tion (Auto-ID) of goods. These technological advancements 
are proving invaluable in scenarios where traditional cloud 
computing falls short, especially under conditions that 
demand high bandwidth and instantaneous feedback. Such 
needs are typical in operations requiring real-time interac­
tions, such as the visual control during the critical phases of 
loading and unloading trucks. This shift towards decentral­
ized computing not only mitigates latency issues but also 
ensures that data processing is closer to the action, result­
ing in quicker decision-making and improved operational 
workflows. Furthermore, the deployment of these technolo­
gies facilitates a more resilient and scalable infrastructure, 
capable of adapting to varying workloads and environmen­
tal conditions, thus setting a standard in logistics.

Abstract
This work introduces an advanced computer vision system designed for real-time auto-identification (Auto-ID) of loads 
in industrial and logistics environments, optimized through a fog computing architecture. The system monitors multiple 
docks in logistics warehouses, identifying pallet loads in real-time and providing feedback for efficient truck loading to 
prevent errors. It enhances traditional Auto-ID by incorporating pallet class classification, detection, and size estimation, 
utilizing foundational models, such as DINOv2, MobileNetV3, SAM, Depth Anything V2, and Depth Pro, alongside 
few-shot learning to generate efficient training datasets with minimal labeling effort. We propose three key innovations: 
(1) an embedding analysis approach for precise load classification; (2) DINOv2-based visual feature detection solutions 
for bounding box estimation, and (3) a depth-guided segmentation strategy for improved load isolation and measurement 
accuracy. Experimental results on a curated industrial dataset compiled by us demonstrate high mean average precision, 
with optimized trade-offs between latency and accuracy for fog computing constraints. This solutions reduces cloud depen­
dency, supports rapid online updates, and ensures robust performance in dynamic logistics settings, making it a scalable 
solution for automated image labeling and load identification in industrial applications.

Expanding on our established technological base, our 
recent developments have introduced a cutting-edge solu­
tion in Auto-ID technologies through computer vision. 
Utilizing innovative Bleecker codes, our existing system 
facilitates real-time identification of goods in motion and 
at a distance [1], thereby significantly reducing the need for 
human intervention. This capability is particularly vital in 
the fast-paced, multifaceted environments typical of logis­
tics operations, such as loading docks. The computer vision 
system we have developed not only increases the accuracy 
of goods tracking but also supports automatic labeling of 
images, which is crucial for ensuring real-time inventory 
accuracy. Furthermore, our system architecture is engi­
neered to monitor multiple docks concurrently, showing 
considerable scalability and adaptability to meet the evolv­
ing demands of modern logistics facilities. This approach 
marks a significant advancement over traditional methods, 
providing a more efficient, accurate, and cost-effective alter­
native to RFID and barcode technologies.
Following the advancements outlined, there is an emerg­
ing need within the logistics sector not merely to identify 
goods but also to discern their content and dimensions to 
ensure accurate labeling. This capability is essential for 
verifying that items are correctly tagged and meet specific 
compliance and regulatory standards before they move 
through the supply chain. Incorporating this functionality 
into our existing system represents a formidable challenge 
that necessitates pushing the boundaries of fog computing 
technologies. By leveraging the distributed nature of fog 
computing, we can process and analyze complex data at 
the edge, closer to where goods are actually handled and 
monitored. This proximity allows for more immediate and 
precise analysis, thus enabling not only the identification 
but also the comprehensive validation of goods in real-time. 
Such integration could significantly enhance operational 
efficiency, reduce errors, and improve compliance with 
shipping and handling regulations. However, for this inte­
gration to truly represent a crucial advancement in intelli­
gent logistics solutions, it must be both rapid and low-effort.
To address this challenge, we present the following work, 
which includes a series of technical contributions designed 
to enhance the capability of our Auto-ID technologies 
within logistics environments. These contributions include:
	
●
Exploration of few-shot learning for low-effort label­
ing and training. This approach is crucial for efficiently 
integrating Auto-ID technologies into existing systems, 
enabling rapid adaptation with minimal labeled data.
	
●
Advanced image classification and object detection 
employing visual foundational models. On the one 
hand, our system employs both MobileNetV3 [2] and 
DINOv2 [3] embeddings combined with simple linear 
probing for precise image classification. Additionally, 
we explore the Segment Anything Model (SAM) [4] 
as an optional module to refine object-level predictions 
and provide enhanced segmentation capabilities. These 
models (especially DINOv2) are becoming widely ap­
plied in modern computer vision systems due to their 
powerful expressiveness, significantly enhancing the 
accuracy and robustness of vision-based operations. In 
fact, on the other hand, we also integrate a set of solu­
tions based exclusively on DINOv2 for both pallet load 
classification and detection.
	
●
Enhanced segmentation through monocular depth 
estimation foundational models. We propose a strat­
egy called depth-guided segmentation, in which mon­
ocular depth estimation is employed to enhance the 
performance of background segmentation models. Spe­
cifically, our system integrates state-of-the-art dense 
prediction models (such as MiDaS [5], Depth Anything 
V2 [6], and Depth Pro [7]) to generate depth cues from 
monocular images. These depth maps are then employed 
to refine the outputs of advanced segmentation networks 
like U2-Net [8], BiRefNet [9], and IS-Net [10], improv­
ing the overall quality and accuracy of the predictions.
	
●
Size estimation using automated segmentation and 
simple pre-calibration. This technique allows for pre­
cise measurement of item dimensions as they move 
through the logistics process, ensuring all goods are not 
only identified but also accurately measured.
	
●
Compilation and curation of a dedicated industrial 
load dataset. To further support research in industrial 
environments, we have compiled and refined a comple­
mentary dataset of approximately 1 000 images, cover­
ing 11 distinct load types. Each image is annotated to 
facilitate the study of load detection and analysis, boost­
ing the use and integration of vision-based models in 
real-world logistics scenarios. By providing this dataset, 
we aim to address the persistent gap in public industrial 
data, which continues to hinder the advancement and 
evaluation of vision-based solutions in logistics.
	
●
Implementation in a real-world scenario within the 
food sector. We have applied these technologies in a 
merchandise shipping plant, proving the practical appli­
cability and effectiveness of our innovations in enhanc­
ing operational efficiency in high-stakes settings.

2  Related work
Fog computing. The paradigm of fog computing has 
recently emerged as an essential solution in industrial envi­
ronments, characterized by applications that demand rapid 
response times [11]. This approach extends cloud capabili­
ties to the network edge, which is particularly crucial for 
computer vision applications. The need to process large vol­
umes of real-time video streaming data makes continuous 
data transfer to cloud servers impractical, subject to inher­
ent latency and potential transmission bottlenecks [12]. Fog 
computing significantly reduces these problems, enhancing 
operational efficiency, critical in industrial settings where 
rapid and accurate decision-making can directly influence 
productivity, process control, and operational safety [13]. 
Our prior work [1] heavily applies this paradigm to process 
full-resolution streams from multiple cameras at ∼25 fps, 
accurately decoding Bleecker codes in real-time.
Computer vision in logistics. The integration of com­
puter vision in logistics has led to significant advancements 
in operational efficiency across various domains, includ­
ing defect detection, inventory management, and qual­
ity control. Recent studies highlight the use of machine 
vision for detecting defects in conveyor belts, improving 
predictive maintenance processes [14]. Additionally, real-
time space occupancy monitoring using computer vision 
enhances warehouse management and optimizes resource 
allocation [15]. Furthermore, computer vision systems are 
being applied for automated quality inspection in produc­
tion environments, increasing precision and reducing opera­
tional costs [16]. Ongoing developments in vehicle tracking 
systems are also improving fleet management by ensuring 
compliance with safety standards and enhancing operational 
efficiency [17, 18]. A key challenge in deploying these sys­
tems is ensuring they generalize across diverse and chang­
ing industrial settings. To this end, research has focused on 
domain adaptation techniques as a critical path for advanc­
ing industrial object detection [19, 20]. These advancements 
confirm the disruptive impact of computer vision on logis­
tics, enabling efficient, reliable, and secure operations.
Foundational models. However, not all modern deep 
learning computer vision models are capable of efficiently 
processing such vast amount of information at those rates, 
even on servers located near the edge. This is especially true 
for the most advanced foundational models, which have 
become recently prominent in the field. These models are 
pretrained on extensive, diverse datasets and are designed 
to capture rich visual features, generalizable across various 
application domains. Notable examples include BYOL [21] 
and MAE [22], with the latest being DINOv2 [3]. In this 
context, several recent works have introduced refinements 
to the DINOv2 framework itself, including modifications at 
the architectural level [23] and alternative training strategies 
[24]. In addition, the model has been successfully applied 
across a variety of tasks such as anomaly detection [25], 
vision-language alignment [26], and visual geometry rea­
soning [27], further demonstrating its broad applicability 
and impact. Most of these models rely on visual transform­
ers (ViT) and are trained applying self-supervised learning, 
minimizing the need for labeled training images. They are 
versatile across numerous computer vision tasks like clas­
sification, segmentation, and 3D depth estimation, requir­
ing only minimal task-specific post-training. Deep learning 
enables these models to provide reusable visual representa­
tions through techniques like few-shot learning [28, 29] and 
fine-tuning using linear probing [30]. Moreover, DINOv2 
has shown remarkable robustness to challenging visual 
conditions, including significant variations in illumination, 
as evidenced both by our experiments on diverse private 
industrial datasets and by recent external studies [31].
Within deep learning architectures, segmentation models 
represent a significant category, offering more precise pixel-
level predictions compared to conventional object detectors. 
These models encompass both ViT-based approaches and 
more traditional convolutional neural networks (CNNs). 
Among the ViT-based methods, SAM [4] stands out for its 
remarkable adaptability across various domains, leveraging 
user-provided prompts. In contrast, BiRefNet [9], another 
ViT-based model, operates without the need for explicit 
prompts and is designed for high-resolution image seg­
mentation. On the other hand, several segmentation mod­
els based on CNNs, such as U2-Net [8] and IS-Net [10], 
offer computational efficiency and do not require explicit 
prompts. These CNN-based models have shown strong per­
formance in dichotomous image segmentation (DIS) [10].
In addition to segmentation models, recent advancements 
in monocular depth estimation have led to significant prog­
ress. These models predict the distance of each pixel relative 
to the camera, providing valuable insights into the 3D struc­
ture of a scene. When combined with other tools, this depth 
information can enhance performance in various tasks, 
including image segmentation. Notably, models such as 
MiDaS [5], Depth Anything V2 [6], and Depth Pro [7], have 
proved notable capabilities in zero-shot depth estimation.

which often suffice for tasks like image classification in fog

expressiveness, combining well-understood, lightweight 
CNN backbones for baseline tasks with state-of-the-art 
foundational models that unlock advanced capabilities cru­

solutions combine both traditional and modern computer 
vision approaches, with the latter being predominant.
Indeed, we evaluate our system using both a traditional 
CNN backbone (MobileNetV3) and a more modern ViT-
based foundational model (DINOv2) for computing global 
embedding vectors. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the 
high expressive power of these vectors enables an exceed­

probing techniques, ideally suited to the fog computing par­
adigm. We also include solutions based solely on DINOv2 
with supervised approaches (but always with very few 
labeled data), marker-assisted, or unsupervised, which we 
have proven to be an excellent option for classifying, detect­

enhanced through the integration of complementary mod­

mation and segmentation models extract valuable insights 
directly from raw input data, eliminating the need for fine-
tuning or supervised retraining.

While few-shot learning has been extensively studied in

and model architectures [34]. Other approaches leverage 
few-shot segmentation to enable compositional reasoning 
in mechanical anomaly detection [35], or combine feature 
enhancement and image generation to improve inspection 
quality with minimal labeled data [36]. In this direction, our 
previous work [18] already explored few-shot learning in 
the context of vision-based logistics operations, highlight­
ing its potential in low-data regimes. These examples high­
light the increasing integration of few-shot techniques as 
effective solutions across computer vision applications.
Auto-ID technologies in logistics. Traditional Auto-ID 
systems in industrial logistics are predominantly based on 
barcodes and RFID technologies. Barcodes, while inex­
pensive and easy to deploy, require direct line-of-sight and 
manual scanning, limiting their suitability for high-through­
put scenarios. RFID systems offer improvements such as 
non-line-of-sight operation and batch reading capabilities, 
but introduce higher deployment costs and reliability issues, 
especially in metal-rich or humid environments [37, 38]. 
Furthermore, neither technology provides access to seman­
tic or spatial context, limiting their effectiveness in modern, 
high-variability logistics operations.
In contrast, vision-based Auto-ID systems leverage 
camera infrastructure and machine learning techniques to 
extract richer information from the environment, includ­
ing object class, position, condition, and interactions [39]. 
These systems enable passive, contactless identification and 
are inherently more adaptable to complex scenarios. Our 
approach falls within this category, extending traditional 
Auto-ID with foundational models and geometric reasoning 
capabilities, offering a scalable and context-aware alterna­
tive for modern logistics environments.

segmentation models, also for load detection (Sect. 4.3).

3  Architecture
Figure 1 illustrates the basic system architecture for a typi­
cal industrial plant scenario. The primary sensorization 
infrastructure comprises several cameras strategically posi­
tioned at fixed control points within the production plant. 
These cameras generate RTSP video streams, which are 
captured and continuously analyzed by a server equipped 
with specific H.264/H.265 decoding hardware GPUs and 
sufficient computational resources (RAM and multicore 
CPUs) to handle real-time image processing for all cam­
eras. A Gigabit Ethernet switch serves as the only needed 
network backbone, centralizing the continuous streaming of 
video. The efficient H.264/H.265 video compression used 
by the cameras ensures that the available bandwidth is not 
fully occupied, though this of course depends also on fac­
tors such as the total number of cameras, image resolutions, 
frame rates, and compression qualities.
A typical setup might include 30 to 40 cameras at a corre­
sponding number of shipping docks, transmitting 2.5K reso­
lution video streams at 25 frames per second each. These 
cameras, forming the core of the sensorization system, are 
installed at strategic lateral points and oriented vertically 
in landscape mode. This orientation augments the vertical 
field of view to encompass the entire pallet load at the high­
est possible resolution, fully capturing the area of interest, 
including the Bleecker code and the whole bounding box 
of the pallet load (see some examples later in Fig. 7). The 
whole system operates on a typical fog computing architec­
ture, which positions computation and storage as close as 
possible to the video sources to minimize latency, enhance 
efficiency, and improve stream processing throughput.
The aforementioned server, directly connected to the 
camera sensing infrastructure on the same local network, 
centralizes the majority of the required image processing,

A. Supervised solution (light blue color in Fig. 4). Spe­
cifically, it consists of two phases: one referred to as offline 
training (corresponding to the left block in Fig. 4) and an 
online operational stage in which inference is performed 
using the trained models obtained in the previous stage.
The offline training phase consists of the following steps: 
1.	 Annotation. First, for each load type, we annotate the 
bounding box for a very small number of instances of 
each class we consider. For these experiments, we con­
sidered 6 prototypes per class–after testing different 
options (3, 6, 9, 12)–following our few-shot approach.
2.	 Embedding. We then compute the DINOv2 embedding 
vectors tile by tile for all the labeled images.
3.	 Binary classifier. Leveraging the bounding box annota­
tions, we apply a heuristic that allows us to obtain posi­
tive DINOv2 vectors for the load class, as well as for

To refine segmentation using depth information, we pro­
pose a method based on Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs). 
A GMM is fitted to a representative 10% subsample of the 
depth histogram, ensuring both modeling accuracy and com­
putational efficiency. In our experiments, empirical evalua­
tion indicated that utilizing 5∼10 Gaussian components the 
principal modes of the depth distribution can be adequately 
captured. Regarding the subsample size, we also evaluated 
various percentages and determined that a 10% subsample 
provides a good trade-off between computational speed and 
an accurate representation of the depth distribution, preserv­
ing all relevant information for the segmentation process. 
We then identify the Gaussian component whose mean is 
closest to the depth estimated from the Bleecker code. Its 
spread thus defines the boundaries of the target depth range.
One of the main challenges is then separating the load 
(proof) from nearby elements such as the floor or forklifts, 
which often share similar depth values. To overcome this, 
we use the depth mask obtained via the GMM as an aux­
iliary input: regions outside the selected depth range are 
smoothed using a Gaussian filter, reducing their influence. 
This preprocessed image is then passed to the background 
segmentation models, improving their ability to isolate the 
load accurately. The complete depth-guided segmentation

6  Discussion
We now discuss the main findings from our comprehen­
sive experimental evaluation of the enhanced Bleecker 
computer vision system for real-time Auto-ID in industrial 
logistics. Tested within a prototypical fog computing setup, 
the results confirm the system’s robustness and adaptability 
across diverse operational scenarios. The following discus­
sion highlights what we consider to be the key takeaways 
regarding the effectiveness, practical relevance, and deploy­
ment considerations of the proposed methodologies.
The added value of Auto-ID. The integration of visual 
class identification and approximate pallet size estimation 
significantly enhances the Bleecker system’s monitoring 
capabilities. By leveraging consistent label placement on 
loads, we developed an extremely efficient methodology for 
automatic image labeling, enabling the creation of medium 
to large datasets with minimal manual effort. This approach 
supports precise object detection, classification, and bound­
ing box placement, achieving high accuracy in identifying 
load types and sizes. The system’s ability to detect labeling 
errors further ensures reliability in real-time logistics opera­
tions. Although Auto-ID technology is crucial for some of 
our approaches, we have also proposed solutions in this 
work that can also achieve solid results without Auto-ID.
Linear probing for online adaptability. To ensure 
adaptability in dynamic environments, we propose a light­
weight linear probing scheme that supports online updates 
as new object types or class instances are introduced. This 
approach enables rapid adaptation without the need to retrain 
large models and allows for multiple variations depending 
on the embedding type and image region used. The method 
is lightweight enough to be executed on the fly directly on 
the fog server. Several alternatives have been proposed to 
balance low latency, bounding box precision, and computa­
tional cost. In this context, the Auto-ID setup stands out as 
a well-balanced solution, offering strong performance with 
moderate latency. Conversely, in fog computing scenarios, 
the additional latency introduced by SAM outweighs its 
accuracy gains, making it a less suitable choice.
DINOv2-powered supervised solutions. These methods 
perform exceptionally well in both binary and multiclass 
settings, achieving mAP scores above 80% in classifica­
tion-based and best-rectangle search configurations for the 
four highest resolutions, and exceeding 90% in the binary 
case for the top three. In contrast, regressor-based super­
vised methods offer lower performance and do not justify 
their added complexity compared to best-rectangle search

Abstract: This work introduces an advanced computer vision system designed for real-time auto-identification (Auto-ID) of loads in industrial and logistics environments, optimized through a fog computing architecture. The system monitors multiple docks in logistics warehouses, identifying pallet loads in real-time and providing feedback for efficient truck loading to prevent errors. It enhances traditional Auto-ID by incorporating pallet class classification, detection, and size estimation, utilizing foundational models, such as DINOv2, MobileNetV3, SAM, Depth Anything V2, and Depth Pro, alongside few-shot learning to generate efficient training datasets with minimal labeling effort. We propose three key innovations: (1) an embedding analysis approach for precise load classification; (2) DINOv2-based visual feature detection solutions for bounding box estimation, and (3) a depth-guided segmentation strategy for improved load isolation and measurement accuracy. Experimental results on a curated industrial dataset compiled by us demonstrate high mean average precision, with optimized trade-offs between latency and accuracy for fog computing constraints. This solutions reduces cloud depen­ dency, supports rapid online updates, and ensures robust performance in dynamic logistics settings, making it a scalable solution for automated image labeling and load identification in industrial applications.
